tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

schema.name: ScheduleWakeup
schema.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Issue #141: Run practice: the last candidate of a budget-bound run goes unreviewed
2	
3	Opened by dat9uy at 2026-11-12T02:21:06Z. Text as of 2026-11-12T03:45:00Z.
4	
5	## Event
6	
7	On 2026-11-12, run 1 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (G-ZBM2RE, PR #140) stopped with its last candidate, H-YXSJEM at `5c5902d`, never reviewed. The two earlier candidates were reviewed, and each review found real defects (10 findings on `10566d4`, 8 on `b4f23b2`). The stop checkpoint says "all review limits closed" and does not name the missing review.
8	
9	The chain, from the run's transcript and the two trees:
10	
11	1. A review finding that is a case of a line becomes a limit, and `--limit` exists only on `hyp record`. So the runner recorded each review as its own Experiment: E-C3GGGJ reviewed `10566d4` and E-7QQ2DP reviewed `b4f23b2`.
12	2. Each candidate therefore cost two Experiments, a gate and a review. The run spent E-HQWTA0, E-C3GGGJ, E-Z5BTZR, E-7QQ2DP and E-NZR3GV (the gate of `5c5902d`), and the stop clause "5 Experiments have been recorded" ended it.
13	3. The default of 5 was set from G-D1CH1R's runs, where every Experiment gates a commit and review findings went straight into fix commits (one Experiment per candidate; run 5 used 4).
14	4. At 17:21:37 the runner wrote "E5 is the last Experiment the budget allows, so this fix commit must close everything." `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` asks for "one review of each candidate commit's diff" before the stop. The prompt's stop clause and the skill conflict, and neither says which yields or that the gap is named at the stop.
15	
16	## Scope
17	
18	Core: the run practice of a Goal whose candidate is a commit (review, budget and stop report) in `hyp-goal-run`, and the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints. No self-review recipe is involved.
19	
20	## Rivals
21	
22	A tree holds this question; each option below is a rival Hypothesis, not a decision. The scenario that separates them: replay the G-ZBM2RE cut after R-8JQPWG (one Experiment left, a fix commit pending) and see whether the run stops with every candidate reviewed or with the gap named.
23	
24	- **H-one-experiment:** a candidate's review is part of its gate Experiment. One Result carries the test verdicts and the review's limits, so a candidate costs one Experiment again.
25	- **H-name-at-stop:** keep the practice; the stop checkpoint names each candidate without a review, so the gap is visible to the owner.
26	- **H-reserve-last:** when one Experiment remains, the runner reviews the current candidate instead of committing another fix, and stops with recorded limits.
27	- **H-raise-budget:** the default of `--experiments` rises (for example to 7) to fit a gate and a review per candidate.
28	
29	These can combine (H-name-at-stop with any other); the tree should say which hold alone.
30	
31	## Done means
32	
33	- A tree under this issue selects a rival, or a combination, from a run on the scenario above.
34	- After the change, a run that reaches its budget either has a review Result for its final candidate or names that candidate as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.
35	
36	Part of #113. Observation log: run 1, entry R10.
37	
38	---
39	
40	Comment by the owner at 2026-11-12T03:04:10Z:
41	
42	Second event, 2026-11-12: run 2 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (actor `claude-g113-2`, session `d3fe6332`) ended the same way, with its last candidate unreviewed.
43	
44	It started with a fresh budget of 5 (`hyp prompt`'s clause "5 Results recorded under the actor") and spent it as:
45	
46	1. R-0E8PFH applies the owner's six answers.
47	2. R-KYKWH9 reviews `5c5902d`, closing run 1's gap; 1 limit.
48	3. R-28A8NB gates the fix commit `2284172`.
49	4. R-3YJ7T2 reviews `2284172`; 2 limits, and the run's own probes of both cases pass.
50	5. R-356DV0 gates `3cfd08d`, a commit that adds tests and spec text for those two passing cases.
51	
52	`3cfd08d` (H-FQ103R) is unreviewed. Unlike run 1, the stop names the gap: "3cfd08d needs a fresh review of its diff, and the cap left no room to run one."
53	
54	What this adds to the rivals:
55	
56	- **Against H-raise-budget.** A fresh budget did not help. Each review so far has led to a new commit (findings 10, 8, 1, 2), and each commit owes its own review, so any fixed budget ends on an unreviewed commit unless a review leads to no commit.
57	- **For H-reserve-last.** The last commit was not needed: both limits' probes passed on `2284172`, so a Result closing them on H-YTD2JG followed by the select would have ended on a reviewed candidate. A related rule to test with it: a case whose check already passes closes as a limit, not with a new commit.
58	- **H-name-at-stop** happened without a rule this time; the scenario should still check whether it holds when the runner is not prompted by an earlier gap.
59	
60	Observation log entry R14.

65	
66	Premise behind the rivals: no text says a review is its own Experiment.

70	- The glossary's Verifier entry (ADR 0015): "Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit."
71	- replay-spec §2: "a Result names the limits it found", and an Experiment is "a pre-registered Result" (ADR 0018). So a finding recorded as a limit needs a Result, and a Result needs an Experiment.
72	- The sort rule "a case of a line is a `--limit`". On `main` it is in no skill: it came from `hyp-owner-grill`'s old hand-off, which told the grill to write it into the `/goal` prompt. On `feat/goal-prompt`, run 1 moved it into `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` (lines 34 and 35) in its own candidate commit `10566d4`.
73	
74	What no text says, and run 1 chose (run 2 copied):
75	
76	- A review is a separate Experiment (E-C3GGGJ, E-7QQ2DP, E-H98Z3B, E-2A0909: `--recipe none --rubric reading`, the candidate as target, probes as evidence), not part of the candidate's gate Experiment.
77	- That Experiment, and its Result, counts against the run's budget.
78	- Its Result gives a verdict on the candidate.
79	
80	So the only written review practice is text the candidate under test wrote, unreviewed and unmerged. Whichever rival this issue selects, `hyp-goal-run` should state how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget, so the next run does not invent it again.

A test-strength question about a one-assertion diff almost always finds one more mutation that slips past, so every review so far has yielded a commit.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: hyp-goal-run
3	description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
4	---
5	
6	The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.
7	
8	## Start
9	
10	- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
11	- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
12	- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
13	- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
14	- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.
15	
16	## Work
17	
18	Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.
19	
20	- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
21	- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
22	- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
23	- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.
24	
25	## Build Goals
26	
27	A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:
28	
29	- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
30	- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
31	- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
32	- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
33	- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
34	- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
35	- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
36	- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.
37	
38	## Before a trade-off
39	
40	Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.
41	
42	## Readings
43	
44	- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
45	- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
46	- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
47	- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:
48	
49	  ```text
50	  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
51	  ```
52	
53	  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.
54	
55	## Owner answers
56	
57	- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
58	- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
59	- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
60	- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.
61	
62	## Reassess
63	
64	Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.
65	
66	1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
67	2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
68	3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
69	4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
70	5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
71	6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.
72	
73	## Goal lines
74	
75	- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
76	- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.

file.content:
---
name: hyp-goal-run
description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
---

The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.

## Start

- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.

## Work

Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.

- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.

## Build Goals

A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:

- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.

## Before a trade-off

Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.

## Readings

- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:

  ```text
  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
  ```

  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.

## Owner answers

- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.

## Reassess

Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.

1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.

## Goal lines

- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.
- A line is never edited. What a line means is a reading. A line no test within the Goal can run is a refer, and the owner accepts or returns it. A new line or a new purpose is a new Goal, so a new tree: tell the owner, and do not write it.

## Stop

Stop on the clauses the `/goal` prompt names. Stopping is not success.

1. Before your last message, record a runner checkpoint, so the fork does not live only in chat; the owner reads `hyp status`, which prints the last checkpoint, each reading in full and what each copy's answer can touch. Do not restate a reading's meanings in the checkpoint:

   ```text
   hyp checkpoint --goal <goal-id> --summary "Stopped: <stop clause>. Waiting for the owner: <the keys under AWAITING OWNER>. Out-of-Goal findings: <one short phrase each, or none>" --why "<why>"
   ```

   An out-of-Goal finding is a case of none of the Goal's lines: it gets no limit, no refer and no reading, and it never holds the select. Name each one in the checkpoint so it lives in the log, not only in chat. A defect in text you changed and may edit is not one: fix it with a commit before the stop.

2. Your last message repeats the checkpoint, and lists each line under LINES by its key, with the Results that ran it, and names each question where OWED still owes a line. A run that ends with lines owed is a normal result.

3. Then list every owner item with the exact command the owner runs: each item under AWAITING OWNER, each out-of-Goal finding (a new Goal or an issue), merging the PR, reinstalling hyp, and each personal skill that names a command the change altered.

## Never

- Never change the Goal or its met rule.
- Never record a choice the owner reserved, and never record an owner answer unless the owner gave those words in this session.

1	---
2	name: hyp-goal-run
3	description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
4	---
5	
6	The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.
7	
8	## Start
9	
10	- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
11	- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
12	- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
13	- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
14	- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.
15	
16	## Work
17	
18	Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.
19	
20	- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
21	- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
22	- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
23	- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.
24	
25	## Build Goals
26	
27	A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:
28	
29	- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
30	- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
31	- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
32	- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
33	- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
34	- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
35	- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
36	- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.
37	
38	## Before a trade-off
39	
40	Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.
41	
42	## Readings
43	
44	- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
45	- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
46	- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
47	- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:
48	
49	  ```text
50	  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
51	  ```
52	
53	  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.
54	
55	## Owner answers
56	
57	- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
58	- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
59	- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
60	- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.
61	
62	## Reassess
63	
64	Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.
65	
66	1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
67	2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
68	3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
69	4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
70	5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
71	6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.
72	
73	## Goal lines
74	
75	- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
76	- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.
77	- A line is never edited. What a line means is a reading. A line no test within the Goal can run is a refer, and the owner accepts or returns it. A new line or a new purpose is a new Goal, so a new tree: tell the owner, and do not write it.
78	
79	## Stop
80	
81	Stop on the clauses the `/goal` prompt names. Stopping is not success.
82	
83	1. Before your last message, record a runner checkpoint, so the fork does not live only in chat; the owner reads `hyp status`, which prints the last checkpoint, each reading in full and what each copy's answer can touch. Do not restate a reading's meanings in the checkpoint:
84	
85	   ```text
86	   hyp checkpoint --goal <goal-id> --summary "Stopped: <stop clause>. Waiting for the owner: <the keys under AWAITING OWNER>. Out-of-Goal findings: <one short phrase each, or none>" --why "<why>"
87	   ```
88	
89	   An out-of-Goal finding is a case of none of the Goal's lines: it gets no limit, no refer and no reading, and it never holds the select. Name each one in the checkpoint so it lives in the log, not only in chat. A defect in text you changed and may edit is not one: fix it with a commit before the stop.
90	
91	2. Your last message repeats the checkpoint, and lists each line under LINES by its key, with the Results that ran it, and names each question where OWED still owes a line. A run that ends with lines owed is a normal result.
92	
93	3. Then list every owner item with the exact command the owner runs: each item under AWAITING OWNER, each out-of-Goal finding (a new Goal or an issue), merging the PR, reinstalling hyp, and each personal skill that names a command the change altered.
94	
95	## Never
96	
97	- Never change the Goal or its met rule.
98	- Never record a choice the owner reserved, and never record an owner answer unless the owner gave those words in this session.

The `dq.select` event that records one Hypothesis as a DesignQuestion's answer. It is written by whoever runs the tree, never in the owner's role. The select is the gate: `hyp select` admits it only when the ledger owes a `select` of that Hypothesis or the owner's `choose` on the question, and otherwise refuses, naming what is owed ([spec §5.1](replay-spec.md#51-write-time-refusals)). An admitted select answers the question while it stands ([spec §7.4](replay-spec.md#74-designquestion-state)); a
_Avoid_: pick, choose (the owner chooses; the select records it), accept, decide (alone)

**Confirm**:
Retired by ADR 0019. It was the `confirm` event in which a role judged a select `sufficient` or `insufficient`; the last use was the owner's confirm of a scope-change select. `hyp confirm` exits 2. An old owner confirm replays only the limits it accepted ([spec §4](replay-spec.md#4-event-types-closed-set)), and an old verifier confirm applies nothing. The owner still "confirms" in plain speech when they choose or accept.
_Avoid_: approve, review; verdict (alone: a confirm's answer was a confirm verdict)

**Decision**:
A DesignQuestion's current Select, its select history and conflicts, and the candidates when the select applied.
_Avoid_: answer (`answered` is a status)

**Dossier**, **Lapse**:
Retired by ADR 0019. The Dossier was the evidence an owner Confirm judged, and a Confirm lapsed when it changed. With no confirm left, nothing reads it: a select stands until a new candidate reopens its question.

**Verifier**:
Retired by ADR 0015. It was the role that confirmed every select, independently of the actor who made it. Old verifier confirms replay as history and apply nothing, and `hyp confirm` is retired (ADR 0019). Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit. In code: `event.RoleVerifier`, read only from old logs.
_Avoid_: reviewer, checker (as a role)

content.text:
I've read issue #141 and its three comments, `hyp-goal-run`, `hyp prompt`, and the G-ZBM2RE tree. I checked the facts below against the source. I've written nothing yet.

**Facts checked**
- **Budget counts Results.** The stop clause counts "Results recorded under the actor" (`internal/cli/prompt.go:167`), not Experiments.
  - A second Result under the same Experiment costs a unit just as a second Experiment does.
  - So H-one-experiment has to be "one Result carries both the gate and the review". An Experiment that holds two Results doesn't fix the cost.
- **The scenario can be replayed.** `hyp status G-ZBM2RE --as-of R-8JQPWG` works. It shows the cut with no live candidate (b4f23b2 contradicted) and a fix commit pending.
- **A review can't be told from a gate in the log.** Both are `--recipe none --rubric reading` Experiments with the candidate as target.
  - So "final candidate has no review" can't be derived or warned on by the binary. It would need a new stored marker.
  - I'm not proposing one. Say so if you want a typed review tested as a rival.
- **Where the "limit" step comes from.** The sort rule "a case of a line is a `--limit`" is in `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md:34-35`. Nothing there says how a review is recorded or what it costs.

## Round 1

**1. Where does this Goal live?**
- **Today:** the repository has five stores. `investigations/goal-prompt` holds G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE, both complete. The scenario is that store's own cut.
- **Option A, same store:** a third Goal in `investigations/goal-prompt`, linked to #113. The run replays `--as-of R-8JQPWG` in place.
- **Option B, new tree:** `investigations/goal-run-review`. The run would have to copy the cut out of the other store.
- **My recommendation:** A. The scenario is that store's history, and one store may hold many Goals.
- I also need your actor name, for example `owner-dat`.

**2. What end state must a budget-bound run guarantee? (this decides the lines)**
- **Today:** the issue's "Done means" is a disjunction. The run ends with a review Result for its final candidate, or the stop checkpoint names it as unreviewed.
- **Option A, the disjunction only.**
  - *Example:* on the R-8JQPWG cut, the run commits the fix, spends its last Result on the gate, and writes "3cfd08d unreviewed". That passes.
  - *Principle:* the gap must be visible.
  - *Effect:* H-name-at-stop alone satisfies this, so the line barely separates the rivals.
- **Option B, the disjunction plus a second line.**
  - *Example:* on run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS, N1 and P1 already pass their probes. The run must end with a review Result for the final candidate and no new commit.
  - *Principle:* a named gap is the floor. Where a reviewed end is reachable, a run must reach it.
  - *Effect:* H-name-at-stop alone and H-raise-budget alone fail it, which matches your run-2 argument.
- **My recommendation:** B. The second line states the outcome, not a mechanism, so H-probe-closes and H-reserve-last stay rivals.

**3. Does `hyp-goal-run` have to state how a review is recorded and what it costs?**
- You wrote that whichever rival wins, the skill should say this.
- *Example of the line:* a consumer given only the skill answers "how do I record a review, and does it use a Result of my budget?" the same way as the selected rule.
- *Principle:* a practice the next run would otherwise invent must be written down.
- **My recommendation:** yes, as a `[P]` line checked by an eval case against the baseline skill's sha256.

**4. Which of the rival Hypotheses does the run test?**
- Your six rivals answer three different questions. One DesignQuestion holds one question, so I'd split them:
  - **Q-A, how a run spends its last Result:** H-one-experiment (one Result carries gate and review), H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last, H-raise-budget.
  - **Q-B, when a review finding costs a commit:** H-probe-closes vs the status quo, where a passing probe is still recorded as a limit.
  - **Q-C, what the final review reads:** H-whole-candidate (cumulative diff from the Goal's base) vs the status quo (latest increment).
- Q-B and Q-C each need two rivals, so the status quo is one of them.
- Per the grill rules, I'm not asking you to choose between these. The question is whether the run should test all of them. Your run-2 argument against H-raise-budget is argued, not tested.
- Combinations: I'd have the run add one only if no single rival holds the lines. H-name-at-stop is the likely partner. The tree then records which hold alone.
- **My recommendation:** test all six, with combinations only on that condition.

**5. The Goal's own run has this defect.** It will gate and review each candidate under the same stop clause, and the default is 5. What `--experiments` value should the hand-off use?
- It's a process preference, so it goes in the `/goal` prompt, not a line.
- **My recommendation:** 10. The run records up to 10 Results, and each rival commit costs a gate and a review under the current practice.

**Lines I plan to write (for routing, not yet confirmed):**
- `[P]` on the R-8JQPWG cut, the run ends with a review Result for its final candidate or a stop checkpoint naming it unreviewed. The baseline skill (sha256) differs.
- `[P]` on run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS, where every found case passes its probe, the run ends with a review Result for its final candidate and no commit for those cases.
- `[P]` `hyp-goal-run` states how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget.
- `[P]` G-ZBM2RE's lines 1-5 and 7 still hold on the candidate, and `go test`, `go vet` and skillcheck pass.

Before I write anything, I still owe the second-reader pass, the preflight scan and the routing table you confirm.

# Context Engineering

Finish the requested work correctly with less wasted context, cost, time and agent
steps. Optimize complete outcomes, including failures, retries and verification.
Never cut required scope or verification to meet an efficiency target.

## Operating loop

1. **Frame:** identify the outcome, constraints and acceptance checks. Reuse an
   accepted plan. Short tasks need no additional plan or ledger ceremony.
2. **Observe:** use available runtime telemetry. Distinguish context occupancy,
   cumulative task spend, provider quota and dollar cost. Missing values are unknown.
3. **Allocate:** reserve room for the next result, response and checkpoint. Reserve
   task budget for verification and integration before assigning independent work.
4. **Execute:** search for the owner, read a sufficient logical unit, bound tool
   output while preserving errors, and record decisions/evidence worth retaining.
5. **Reassess:** expand only when evidence is missing; stop exploration when acceptance
   is met. Checkpoint before a step likely to exceed headroom or when context degrades.

## Proportional hygiene

- Search before large reads (roughly 2k tokens is a hint, not a prohibition).
  Read whole files when their structure or cross-cutting contract is the question.
- Keep a small current-state ledger for long work: observed facts with source/revision,
  decisions with reasons, open uncertainties, and next action. Do not log every read.
- Reuse verified facts until the source, revision, environment or decision changes.
  Refresh changed or consequential live state; line numbers alone are not identity.
- Prefer native output limits or structured filters. For shell logs, preserve the
  producer exit status, retain a full log when necessary, and report truncation.
  Follow the safe pattern in [session protocol](references/session-protocol.md).
- Batch independent bounded calls, inspect every result, and keep dependent operations
  sequential. Limit the aggregate output too; batching is not free context capacity.
- Retry a transient failure within a bounded policy/backoff. For deterministic errors,
  change the cause before retrying. Recheck when relevant state changes.
- Run focused checks first; broaden when required by repository gates or risk.
  Keep useful progress updates; avoid repeating plans and dumping results.
- Load one reference per current question. Instructions from the runtime or project
  still take precedence over this skill's efficiency heuristics.

## Cache and cost observations

When the host exposes them, record input/output tokens, cache reads/writes, elapsed time,
retries and cost per successful task with model/runtime/settings and source identity.
Missing telemetry remains `null`/unknown, never estimated from file length. Context occupancy
is not cumulative billed tokens or currency. Prefix stability, cache policy and reasoning
effort belong to prompt assembly/adapters or APIs; renaming a skill does not establish a
cache improvement. Compare matched original/candidate runs before changing runtime defaults.

content.text:
Answers to your two questions, then round 2. I've written nothing.

## How each line serves your two aims

| Line | Aim 1: the review can't easily run out of budget | Aim 2: the review doesn't go on over small changes |
|---|---|---|
| L1 `[P]` R-8JQPWG cut (one Result left, fix pending): the run ends with a review Result for its final candidate, or the stop checkpoint names it unreviewed | Yes. This is the exhaustion case, and the named gap is the floor. | No |
| L2 `[P]` R-JHBCWS cut (N1 and P1 pass their probes): the run ends with a review Result for its final candidate and no commit for those cases | Yes. It requires a reviewed end where one is reachable. | Yes, it's the only line that stops a loop. It pins that a case whose probe passes causes no commit. |
| L3 `[N]` cost: a candidate's cost exceeds 1.5 times the base's at the same starting point | Indirectly. It stops "fix" by reserving unlimited review. | Yes. It caps what a longer loop can cost. |
| L4 `[P]` the skill states how a review is recorded and whether it counts | Yes. A run that knows the cost can plan for it. | Partly. A run that knows a review is one Result doesn't invent a second Experiment. |
| L5 `[P]` G-ZBM2RE lines 1-5 and 7, `go test`, `go vet` and skillcheck still pass | No, it's a guard. | No, it's a guard. |

**Gap.** Aim 2 rests on L2 and L3 only. L2 covers a finding whose probe passes. It does not cover a finding whose probe fails but is small, like a one-assertion fix. That case can still loop: fix, review, another small fix.

A line for it would be: *"on each cut, after a review round whose cases all pass or are closed, no further review round is owed."* I'm not sure it can be pinned without naming the mechanism. If you want it, tell me and I'll draft it in the routing table. Without it, a small real defect legitimately costs one more commit.

## Cost and the median

I'd define it so it can be computed from a trial's transcript and doesn't depend on price changes.

- **Trial cost.** The input-equivalent tokens of every model turn from the starting point to the trial's stop (a stop checkpoint, or the stop clause).
  - Weights: input 1, cache-write 1.25, cache-read 0.1, output 5. These are the price ratios relative to input.
  - The weights are pinned in the L3 text. A missing value is unknown, never estimated.
- **Median per (candidate, starting point).** The middle of the 3 trial costs when sorted. For 3 values it's the 2nd.
- **A hang.** A trial that reaches no stop within a wall-clock and turn cap. The cap is fixed in the Experiment's verdict rule before it runs.
  - A hang's cost is infinite. It sorts last, and it's never a number.
  - One hang in 3 leaves the median finite, so one hang doesn't fail a candidate by itself. Two hangs make the median infinite, so the candidate fails.
- **The rule.** A candidate passes if its median ≤ 1.5 × the base's median at the same starting point, and it has at most one hang.
  - If the base's own median is infinite (two or more base hangs), the ratio is undefined. The verdict is `inconclusive`, not a pass.
- **What 3 trials can show.** 3 trials separate large effects only. H-whole-candidate, a one-diff review against many, is such a case. H-probe-closes vs the status quo may not be separable by cost alone, and the run should say so.

## The ak-context-engineering question

It could help. It's not in this repository's `.claude/skills` or in `~/.claude/skills`, only in the agentkit cache (`…/engineer/claude-code/3.0.0/engineer/skills/ak-context-engineering`) and two other projects.

Its guidance matches the method you gave:
- Record input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, elapsed time and retries per successful task.
- Keep the model and settings fixed.
- Treat missing telemetry as unknown.
- Compare matched original and candidate runs.

I read `SKILL.md` but not `references/evaluation.md`. If the Goal uses it, the body's `Read only:` would name that path pinned by sha256, like ak-skill-creator. I'd compute the hashes at write time.

- **The ledger.** `hyp status` lists under OWED what the tree owes and who
  owes it, and marks an item an Experiment aimed at and did not settle
  ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md) §8.1). It is the one account of progress

- **Design marks.** `hyp signals` lists the Experiments set up against no live
  rival (one-rival) or against a dead one (D1). A Result that leaves a
  target without a verdict is refused, not marked (ADR 0018).
- **The select is the gate.** `hyp select` is admitted only when the ledger

## What the second reader changed

Checked and true:
- **L2 was already met at its cut.** At the R-JHBCWS cut, H-FQ103R (`3cfd08d`) is the only candidate and its review is recorded. A run that did nothing would pass L2, so I reworded it to end with the select and no later commit.
- **The two starting points differ in budget and skill text.**
  - Cut 1 (R-8JQPWG) is `claude-g113-1`'s fourth Result, so one is left under a default of 5. The skill there is `a6152711…` (from `b4f23b2`).
  - Cut 2 (R-JHBCWS) is `claude-g113-3`'s first Result, so budget is not the issue there. The skill there is `cb15e2f2…` (from `3cfd08d`), which is also today's main.
  - So each starting point is a store cut plus a repository commit, and each has its own baseline hash.
- **The unit is Results.** `claude-g113-1` recorded 6 Results against a clause of 5.
- **A raised default breaks a closed Goal's pinned text.** `prompt_test.go:55` and `prompt.golden:2` pin "5 Results". L6 now allows that one number to change, with test and golden changing with it.
- **Replay must use the candidate's own default.** If the runs forced `--experiments`, H-raise-budget would be hidden. Each replay uses the original actor, the store at the cut, and the candidate's default.
- **L5 can't be seen in a replay.** The cuts predate the new Goal. L5 is checked by a separate eval case on the skill text.

Preflight scan:
- `docs/how-hyp-improves-itself.md:29` says a run's cap is "stated by the `/goal` prompt or the recipe, not by hyp". That is already wrong, because `hyp prompt` prints a default. Run 4 named it as F8, out of Goal.

## Lines (6, all within the cap)

- **L1 `[P]`:** At the R-8JQPWG cut (repo `b4f23b2`, actor `claude-g113-1`, prompt from the candidate's own `hyp prompt` with its default), each of 3 Sonnet trials ends with a review Result for its final candidate, or a stop checkpoint naming it unreviewed. The baseline skill (sha256 `a6152711c2c930b275583f19dec074205e3eb83deac8d361831fda3566b080ab`) fails this in at least one trial, and the candidate's differs.
- **L2 `[P]`:** At the R-JHBCWS cut (repo `3cfd08d`, actor `claude-g113-3`, where the review's case N1 passes its probe), each trial ends with the select of H-FQ103R and no later candidate commit.
